column4: This ayah joins both sides of the section's image: believers must not turn themselves away from the Messenger (يَرْغَبُوا۟ ... عَن), and every thirst, fatigue (نَصَبٌ), and step borne in God's path is credited as a righteous deed.

Moses first completes the concrete labor of watering for the two women, then withdraws and addresses his Lord as wholly needy for whatever good He sends; it enacts work followed immediately by Godward desire and provision.
The Prophet is commanded قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ, a direct parallel to rising into purposeful labor in 94:7; 74:3 and 74:7 then fix that labor's direction upon his Lord.
وَرَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ fronts “your Lord” before the command, matching the exclusive emphasis of the source section's وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ and supplying the next Godward act after 74:2's rising.
وَلِرَبِّكَ فَٱصْبِرْ makes the Lord the expressly fronted purpose of sustained endurance, so the standing work begun in 74:2 is not directionless strain.
قُمِ ٱلَّيْلَ commands the same Prophet to rise for demanding night worship; 73:7-8 place this rising beside daytime occupation and total direction to the Lord.
The Prophet's long daytime engagement (سَبْحًا طَوِيلًا) supplies the work phase of the cycle whose Godward phase is stated in 73:8.
Remembering the Lord's name and devoting oneself wholly to Him (تَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًا) is a close nonlexical formulation of the source section's exclusive وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَٱرْغَب.

God knows the Prophet and his companions stand through measured portions of the night, then mentions travelers seeking His bounty and fighters in His way; worship, taxing activity, and divine provision remain one directed cycle.
فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ gives the Prophet two strenuous acts expressly “for your Lord,” matching the command pattern and exclusive direction developed from 94:7-8.

When prayer has been completed, believers are to remember God standing, sitting, and lying down; the explicit “when you have finished ... then” sequence closely matches the source section's completion followed by renewed Godward action.
After completing the rites, pilgrims must remember God intensely; the same ayah contrasts that directed remembrance with a person whose request stops at “give us in this world.”
When Friday prayer is finished, believers disperse through the earth seeking God's bounty while remembering Him much, showing that transition into worldly work can itself stay oriented to the Giver.
The call to Friday prayer requires leaving trade and hastening to God's remembrance; together with 62:10 it forms the reverse half of the section's cycle between labor and worship.

When victory and the people's entry have arrived in 110:1-2, the Prophet is told to glorify his Lord and seek His forgiveness, an exact structural parallel to a completed charge opening into fresh devotion.
The Ramadan ruling says to complete the prescribed number and then magnify God for His guidance, directly pairing completion with a Godward act rather than vacancy.

سَنَفْرُغُ لَكُمْ uses the source root ف ر غ of God turning intentionally to the two weighty communities; it confirms the section's developed sense that “becoming free” can mean a deliberate new address.

After the garden is lost, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better and say إِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا رَاغِبُونَ; desire, direction, Lord, and hoped-for abundant gift all coincide.

Instead of making satisfaction depend on a share of alms, the speakers should trust what God and His Messenger give and say إِنَّا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ رَاغِبُونَ; the object of desire shifts from the allotment to God, its giver.

God answers Zechariah, grants John, and repairs his wife because the household hastened in good works and called on Him رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا; hopeful desire is joined to action, fear, humility, and divine gift.
Every human being is laboring painfully toward the Lord (كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ) and will meet Him, making explicit both the exertion and the final direction that 94:7-8 bind together.
A person has only what he strives for; 53:40-42 continue from visible effort and full recompense to the declaration that the endpoint is the Lord.
Human striving will be seen, so the labor named in 53:39 is purposeful and accountable on its way to the Lord's endpoint in 53:42.
The striving of 53:39 will receive the fullest repayment before 53:42 names the Lord as the final end, connecting sustained work with its divine issue.
وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ٱلْمُنتَهَىٰ makes the Lord the endpoint with the same fronted directional phrase that the section hears in وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ٱلرُّجْعَىٰ answers the self-sufficiency of 96:6-7: however a person directs desire now, the return is exclusively to the Lord.
The command to worship one's Lord until certainty comes gives the section's tiring upright devotion its duration: renewed service continues until death.
Whoever hopes to meet his Lord must do righteous work and admit no partner into the Lord's worship; hoped-for encounter, action, and exclusive direction are stated together.
The night devotee prostrates and stands, fears the Hereafter, and hopes for his Lord's mercy; bodily standing is given the paired directions of fear and hope, unlike heedless toil.
Their sides leave their beds as they call upon their Lord in fear and hope, a bodily rising into the same رغبا ورهبا orientation expressed in 21:90.
وَقُومُوا۟ لِلَّهِ قَٰنِتِينَ commands believers to stand devoutly for God, directly joining upright posture to its intended recipient.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing, making strenuous uprightness an enacted relation to the Lord.
The Prophet is told to endure his Lord's judgment and glorify Him when he rises (حِينَ تَقُومُ), joining rising, patience, and praise under the Lord's gaze.
Job calls his Lord when afflicted with نُصْبٍ and torment; the fatigue root developed in the section appears inside a concrete act of Godward appeal.
إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ fronts the sole object of worship and help, clarifying the same exclusivity the section draws from fronting وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
The Prophet declares that his prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are for God, Lord of the worlds, making every act and the whole life cycle share one direction.
“No partner has He” makes the exclusivity of 6:162 explicit and the Prophet says he is commanded to submit, closely matching the source section's “only your Lord.”

Shuayb describes reform as the work he seeks to do, says success comes only through God, and concludes عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ وَإِلَيْهِ أُنِيبُ; effort, enablement, and return have one source and direction.

The Prophet is commanded to recite revelation and say that God alone is his Lord, on Him he relies, and to Him is his return; the repeated إِلَيْهِ gives the section's direction an explicit confessional form.
Abraham and his companions say to God, “upon You we rely, to You we turn, and to You is the destination”; trust, present reorientation, and final arrival are all exclusively Godward.

أَنِيبُوا۟ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ وَأَسْلِمُوا۟ لَهُ commands an intentional turn to the Lord followed by submission before judgment arrives, a direct parallel to purposeful redirection after one phase ends.
فَفِرُّوٓا۟ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ makes movement toward God an urgent command from the Messenger, a vivid nonlexical counterpart to directing all رغبة to the Lord.
Those who exert themselves “for Us” are promised guidance into God's ways; strenuous action is qualified by its recipient and answered with divine guidance.

Believers are commanded to strive for God with the striving due Him, then establish prayer, give alms, and hold fast to Him; exhausting service is explicitly directed and sustained by their Protector.
“Work” is followed by the assurance that God, His Messenger, and believers will see the work and that people will be returned to God; present labor is placed under its final divine destination.
ٱعْمَلُوٓا۟ ءَالَ دَاوُۥدَ شُكْرًا commands David's household to turn the gifts just described into work as gratitude, showing divine bounty generating further directed labor.

The Prophet must remain with those who call their Lord morning and evening desiring His face, and must not look past them seeking worldly adornment; Godward desire and worldward appetite are directly opposed.
Those who call their Lord morning and evening “desiring His face” embody sustained, exclusively directed desire, and the Prophet is commanded not to drive them away.
Patience is undertaken seeking the Lord's face and is joined to prayer, giving, and repelling evil with good; endurance and a chain of acts receive their direction from the Lord.
Whatever good believers spend is to be for seeking God's face and will be repaid in full, linking a concrete act, its exclusive intention, and the giver's return.
Giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due is declared best for those who desire God's face; active generosity becomes the form taken by Godward desire.
Worldly lending meant to increase through people's wealth is set against alms given desiring God's face; the ayah tests desire by both its direction and the kind of increase sought.
The giver acts only in seeking the face of his Lord Most High, an exclusivity reinforced by 92:19's denial that he is merely repaying another person's favor.
Whoever desires the Hereafter, strives for it with the striving due it, and believes has that striving gratefully received; desire's object determines the worth of labor.
The Lord extends His gift (عَطَآءِ رَبِّكَ) to both groups, making Him the source even when human desires diverge and directly recalling the section's “abundant gift” sense of الرغيبة.
The command to observe how divine gifts differ culminates in the greater degrees and favor of the Hereafter, completing 17:18-20's contrast between two directed desires.
The Prophet is promised that his Lord will give until he is satisfied; the Lord as giver of ample bounty concretely fills out the section's dictionary link between رغبة, gift, and Rabb.
وَأَمَّا بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ joins “your Lord” directly to His favor and makes that favor occasion a new command, matching the section's developed ر ب ب sense of blessing and beneficence.
Once the throne is set before Solomon, he immediately names the achievement “from my Lord's favor” and sees it as a test of gratitude, turning a completed feat back toward its Giver.
After the barrier-building work of 18:96-97 is complete, Dhu al-Qarnayn calls it a mercy from his Lord and points to his Lord's future promise, redirecting accomplishment away from himself.
Moses answers the commission to Pharaoh by praying رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى; opened breast, Lord, and readiness for a hard prophetic task meet as they do across 94:1 and 94:7-8.

God opens a breast to Islam for the one He wills to guide, while misdirection makes it constricted as though climbing upward; the root ش ر ح marks a divinely given capacity whose direction is decisive.
A breast God has opened to Islam places its possessor upon light from his Lord; this supplies the Godward content of the opened breast recalled in the section.

Facing battle, the believers ask their Lord to “pour out” (أَفْرِغْ) patience upon them and make their feet firm; the different ف ر غ sense still joins divine address, endurance, and upright steadiness.
The threatened magicians ask their Lord to pour out (أَفْرِغْ) patience and take them as submitters; the root's pouring sense serves steadfast, exclusively Godward endurance under pain.
Trade and sale do not distract these people from God's remembrance, prayer, and alms, so ordinary work remains ordered around worship rather than widening desire toward acquisition.
Believers are told to race in good works and that all will return to God, coupling purposeful activity with the common destination that explains its direction.
No small or large expenditure and no valley crossed in the campaign goes unwritten; it continues 9:120's directed fatigue by showing each further act preserved for the best recompense.

Qarun is told to seek the lasting abode with what God has given him, retain his proper worldly share, and do good as God did good to him; divine gift is deliberately redirected into further good work.
Those who respond to their Lord establish prayer and conduct affairs by consultation while spending from His provision, turning divine response and gift into an ongoing field of work.
The feeders say they act only for God's face and desire no repayment or thanks from people; a concrete service is directed beyond every immediate human return.
Remembering the name of one's Lord and praying supplies the positive Godward acts immediately before 87:16 exposes preference for worldly life.
The Lord of east and west alone is God, so the Prophet is to take Him as trustee; this grounds 73:8's total self-devotion in exclusive lordship.
When his Lord says “Submit,” Abraham says he submits to the Lord of the worlds; this is the positive response immediately following 2:130's question about turning away from Abraham's way.
Abraham withdraws from his father's gods and says he will call upon his Lord, enacting the redirection that 19:46 frames with رَاغِبٌ ... عَنْ.
Zechariah's “My Lord, do not leave me alone” supplies the concrete Godward request answered in 21:90, where his household's prayer is characterized as hope and fear.
عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ presents laboring, exhausted faces whose next destination is the blazing fire in 88:4; it is the section's tiring exertion stripped of its saving Godward direction.
Entering the intensely hot fire supplies the outcome of the exhausted labor in 88:3 and makes its opposition to labor directed toward the Lord concrete.
مَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ uses رغب with عَنْ for turning away, the exact grammatical reversal of the source section's رغب with إِلَىٰ.
Abraham's father asks أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ ءَالِهَتِى, using رغبة with عَنْ for rejection; 19:48 then shows Abraham's positive direction toward his Lord.
The critic of alms is pleased only when given a share and angry when not, embodying desire fixed on distribution; 9:59 replaces that stance with confidence in God's bounty and desire toward God.
Paradise's people are touched by no fatigue (نَصَبٌ) and will never be removed, setting a boundary to the section's present command of tiring, repeated service.
The people settled in the lasting abode praise God because neither fatigue (نَصَبٌ) nor weariness touches them there; directed labor belongs to the journey, not its completed reward.

The erected stones or altars (ٱلْأَنصَابُ) are called satanic filth to avoid; this concrete ن ص ب object reverses the section's uprightness by giving cultic direction to something other than the Lord.
Animals sacrificed upon erected stone altars (ٱلنُّصُبِ) are forbidden, sharply contrasting with 108:2's sacrifice expressly performed for one's Lord.

On resurrection they rush from graves as though racing toward an erected target (نُصُبٍ); the source dictionary's “setting upright” sense appears as a false or merely apparent destination rather than upright service to the Lord.
The one who willingly opens his breast to unbelief (شَرَحَ بِٱلْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا) gives the ش ر ح image the opposite content from a breast opened for prophetic, Godward work.
Whoever desires only the immediate life receives a measured portion and then Hell; it is a precise instance of wide desire being directed toward the nearer world, opposed by 17:19.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in it, so labor can receive its whole horizon from the wrong object of desire.
For the world-seekers of 11:15 only fire remains in the Hereafter and their works become void, supplying the same boundary as the source section's warning about undirected fatigue.

One who desires the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase, while one who desires the worldly harvest receives some of it but no share beyond; the direction of desire governs both work's yield and its permanence.
During a demanding collective charge, some desired the world and others the Hereafter; the ayah shows desire's direction splitting people within the same work.
“You desire the goods of the world, while God desires the Hereafter” directly opposes acquisition-minded desire to the divine direction a prophetic task requires.
The Prophet must turn away from one who turns from God's remembrance and desires only worldly life, combining wrong desire with an enacted turning away from the divine reminder.
Preferring worldly life is the decisive orientation of the transgressor; 79:40-41 oppose it with fear of standing before the Lord and restraint of desire.
Fear of standing before one's Lord restrains the soul from caprice, making the final standing before God govern desire and conduct now.
Paradise becomes the dwelling of the person in 79:40, completing the reversal of 79:38's preference for worldly life.
بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا states the worldly preference that the source's dictionary question attributes to an expansive desire toward acquisition.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, naming the enduring alternative to 87:16's nearer-life preference and correcting desire's scale.
Loving the immediate life states the attraction that pulls desire away from its proper Lordward direction.
Neglecting the Hereafter is the inseparable other side of 75:20's love of the immediate, exposing what world-directed desire leaves behind.
Those people love the immediate life and leave behind them a weighty day, so present preference evades rather than removes the final divine encounter.
Those who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter and obstruct God's way embody desire expanding toward the world until it also bends others' direction.
Preferring worldly life over the Hereafter explains the sealing of hearts, showing how chosen direction can undo the opened, receptive breast.
Those desiring worldly life wish for wealth like Qarun's when he appears in his adornment, a concrete scene of the acquisition-focused رغبة described in the source dictionary.

Those given knowledge answer the wishers of 28:79 that God's reward is better for the believing righteous, but attained by the patient; gift, labor, and endurance are redirected beyond Qarun's display.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and lasting for believers who rely on their Lord; the Giver and the gift are put in their proper order.
Human beings transgress when they regard themselves as self-sufficient; 96:8 answers this false independence with the unavoidable return to the Lord.
Seeing oneself free of need is the inner stance opposed to وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَٱرْغَب, since it imagines no gift or direction beyond the self; 96:8 corrects it.
The heart of Moses' mother becomes فَارِغًا and is then bound firm by God; this distinct “empty” sense of ف ر غ shows that vacancy alone is unstable until the heart is given a sustaining direction.
Moses names the fatigue (نَصَبًا) met on his journey; it is the same bodily weariness developed from ن ص ب, though here the ayah marks travel toward a human teacher rather than worship itself.
Remembering God standing, sitting, and on one's sides shows devotion continuing through every bodily state, closely echoing 4:103 though it lacks that ayah's “after completion” transition.

God is the one who sees the Prophet when he rises; in the surrounding appeal to trust the Mighty and Merciful, this makes prophetic rising accountable to the Lord, though the precise act of rising is not specified in the ayah.
Before declaring their desire toward their Lord in 68:32, the garden owners glorify their Lord and admit wrongdoing, showing the reorientation beginning in confession.
The garden owners first turn toward one another in blame, then in 68:32 turn their hope toward their Lord; the two directions expose the change produced by repentance.
Their admission that they transgressed clears the way for 68:32's hope in a better replacement from their Lord, so the desired gift follows moral recognition rather than mere loss.
Abraham answers his father's threat with peace and promises to ask his Lord's forgiveness; this begins the positive Lordward turn completed in 19:48.
The coming of God's victory marks the completed achievement that triggers the command to glorify and seek forgiveness in 110:3; its relevance depends on that continuation.
Seeing people enter God's religion in crowds supplies the visible fruition of the prophetic task before 110:3 orders a fresh turn to praise and repentance.
“Go to Pharaoh” gives Moses the hard work for which he immediately asks his Lord to open his breast in 20:25; the link is the commission that makes the opening purposeful.
Moses asks his Lord to ease his task after asking for an opened breast, connecting divine enlargement to the labor it enables rather than to rest for its own sake.

Dhu al-Qarnayn directs a sequence of strenuous acts—bring iron, blow, bring molten copper to pour (أُفْرِغْ)—whose finished result he attributes to his Lord's mercy in 18:98; the ف ر غ form itself bears the separate “pour” sense.
Each community has a direction toward which it turns, followed by the command to race in good works and the promise that God will gather all; direction is tested by action and final gathering.

تَرْغَبُونَ أَن تَنكِحُوهُنَّ lacks the preposition that elsewhere tells whether رغبة is toward or away from the orphan women; that grammatical ambiguity specifically illuminates the section's insistence that فِي/إِلَى and عَنْ reverse the verb's direction.
Upon pouring forth from Arafat, pilgrims are told to remember God at the sacred place; the transition from a completed movement into remembrance begins the ritual sequence continued in 2:199-200.
Pilgrims are told to depart where the people depart and then seek God's forgiveness, another completed movement followed by a deliberately Godward act before 2:200's completed rites.
Immediately after 2:200's person who asks only for this world, this speaker addresses “our Lord” for good in both this world and the Hereafter, correcting desire without denying earthly good.

When trade or amusement appears, people leave the Prophet standing; the ayah declares what is with God better and God the best provider, exposing the very worldward diversion that 62:9-10's work-worship cycle must govern.
The most balanced garden owner recalls that he had urged the others to glorify God; this is the first explicit summons away from acquisitive plotting and toward the Lord before 68:29-32.
When God's servant stands calling upon Him, the crowd nearly masses around him; standing and Godward invocation coincide in a scene especially close to “rise, exert yourself, and desire your Lord.”
The Prophet is commanded to keep an additional night vigil, with the hope that his Lord will raise him to a praised station; taxing worship, hoped-for divine gift, and rising are linked.
At the culmination of Joseph's long work and reunion, he names dominion and knowledge as his Lord's gifts, then asks the Creator to take him in submission and join him to the righteous.
At full maturity, the person asks his Lord for power to thank Him for His favor and to do righteous work pleasing to Him; received bounty becomes fresh, expressly directed labor.
Solomon responds to a bestowed ability by asking his Lord to enable gratitude, righteous work pleasing to Him, and entry into His mercy; gift, work, and desire all return to the Giver.

Dhu al-Qarnayn says what his Lord has established him in is better than the offered payment and asks the people to help with strength; the barrier project begins by preferring divine provision and directing collective labor.
The Lord of the heavens and earth is to be worshipped with steadfast perseverance in His worship, giving the section's repeated tiring service both its object and its sustaining command.
The Prophet must command his household to pray and persevere in it; God asks no provision from them but provides for them, sharply ordering exertion, desire, and gift around the Lord.
The Prophet says he is commanded to worship God with religion made sincere for Him, a direct statement of the exclusive direction expressed by the source section's fronted “to your Lord.”
The Prophet declares that God is the one he worships, making his devotion sincere for Him; the fronted object gives the same exclusive force as the section's وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
People were commanded only to worship God sincerely and uprightly, establish prayer, and give alms; exclusive orientation issues in repeated concrete acts.
Believers are commanded to call upon God with religion sincere for Him even when unbelievers dislike it, making exclusive Godward appeal a deliberate stance under opposition.
Because the Living One alone is God, people are commanded to call upon Him sincerely and praise the Lord of the worlds; exclusive address and lordship are joined explicitly.
Setting one's face at every place of worship and calling God with sincere religion turn bodily direction and invocation into a repeated exclusive practice.
Abraham turns his face toward the Creator of heavens and earth as an upright monotheist and rejects association, a vivid enacted counterpart to directing desire only toward the Lord.
The Prophet is commanded to set his face toward the religion uprightly and not be among the associators, expressing exclusive orientation as a sustained posture.
The command to set one's face toward the religion uprightly makes directedness itself the governing image of faithful action.
Whoever submits his face to God while doing good has his reward with his Lord; orientation, action, and divine recompense appear in one formulation.
The best religious course is to submit one's face to God while doing good and following Abraham, joining Godward orientation with active excellence.
One who submits his face to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold, and the outcome of all matters is to God; present action and final direction coincide.
Abraham says, “I am going to my Lord; He will guide me,” making movement toward the Lord both an intentional departure and an expectation of divine provision.
The tranquil soul is commanded to return to its Lord, satisfied and pleasing; the final Godward turn fulfills directed desire in mutual contentment.
The believer must follow the path of one who turns to God, and all will return to Him; chosen present direction is placed inside the unavoidable final return.
Those who avoid serving false powers and turn to God receive good news, giving the positive redirection that contrasts with the erected cult objects condemned in 5:90.
God chooses whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back, so deliberate reorientation toward Him is answered by divine guidance.
God guides to Himself whoever turns back, a concise promise that Godward direction draws a corresponding gift of guidance.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring good deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; what is acquired is contrasted with work whose value remains before its Giver.

When called to go forth in God's path, some grow heavy toward the earth and prefer worldly life to the Hereafter; downward attachment and refusal of effort directly reverse the command to rise and labor toward the Lord.

Family, acquired wealth, feared commercial loss, and pleasing homes must not become dearer than God, His Messenger, and striving in His way; the ayah tests worldly acquisition against directed exertion.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from God's remembrance, a specific boundary keeping ordinary concerns inside the cycle of Godward attention.
A person gives up his very self seeking God's pleasure, making arduous action the embodied form of exclusively directed desire.
Those who spend their wealth seeking God's pleasure and inner firmness are compared to a garden yielding multiplied produce; direction, work, and abundant return are concretely connected.
Private counsel gains great reward when its charity, recognized good, or reconciliation is done seeking God's pleasure; the intended recipient determines the worth of practical work.
The Prophet's companions are seen bowing and prostrating while seeking bounty and pleasure from God, joining strenuous worship to the desire for divine gift.
The poor emigrants lose homes and wealth while seeking bounty and pleasure from God and supporting His cause, a concrete case of exhausting labor directed beyond worldly acquisition.
God offers a “trade” that saves from punishment, deliberately recasting the world of acquisition as an exchange whose direction and gain are divine.
The saving trade consists of faith and striving with wealth and lives in God's way, making costly work the concrete expression of the desire introduced in 61:10.
Reciting God's book, establishing prayer, and spending from His provision are people’s hope for a trade that will never perish; work and commerce are redirected toward lasting divine return.
“Your striving is diverse” states the problem at the heart of the section: exertion takes its value from the direction disclosed in the alternatives of 92:5-10.
The person who gives and remains mindful begins the positive course of striving whose outcome is ease in 92:7.
Affirming the best promise supplies the believed destination that distinguishes the giver's striving before 92:7 promises facilitation toward ease.
God will ease the giver and believer toward ease, linking the direction of effort in 92:5-6 with the ease that God provides.
Believers are commanded to bow, prostrate, worship their Lord, and do good so that they may prosper; bodily worship and useful work lead directly into 22:78's striving for God.
Believers must be mindful of God, seek a means toward Him, and strive in His way; direction toward God and strenuous activity are expressly combined.

Sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God, but piety does; the animals were subjected so believers may magnify Him, clarifying that an act's Godward direction lies in its intention rather than its material output.
The Lord answers the callers that He never lets any worker's work be lost, then names migration, expulsion, suffering, and fighting before promising reward from Himself.

A person in distress calls God lying, sitting, or standing, then passes on after relief as though never calling; temporary bodily orientation under need reverses the section's continuing cycle of devotion.
At sea, danger strips away every invoked object except God, but safe arrival on land is followed by turning away; the scene exposes an unstable, crisis-bound Godward direction.
When harm touches a person he calls his Lord turning to Him, but after divine favor he forgets and assigns rivals; gift becomes the occasion for reversed desire rather than renewed service.
People call their Lord while turning to Him under harm, yet after tasting mercy some associate partners; the change of circumstance reveals a direction that does not endure.
Whoever desires worldly reward receives from it and whoever desires Hereafter reward receives from it; the desired recompense distinguishes two orientations within mortal action.
Anyone desiring worldly reward is reminded that both worldly and Hereafter reward are with God, redirecting desire from one limited gift to the Giver who possesses both.
A catalog of desired people, treasure, animals, and fields is identified as worldly enjoyment, a concrete expansion of the section's “wide desire” to acquire the world.
Against 3:14's desired possessions, the Prophet asks whether he should announce something better: lasting gardens, purity, and pleasure with their Lord.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting; gift is distinguished from its enduring source.
The question about the greatest losers in works prepares a direct case of effort whose direction makes it futile, specified in 18:104.
Their striving goes astray in worldly life while they think they are doing well, a precise counterpart to exhausted work that never reaches its proper Lordward end.

Worldly life is play, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children whose growth withers, while the Hereafter holds punishment or divine forgiveness and pleasure; acquisitive effort is measured by what remains.

Monasticism was innovated while seeking God's pleasure, yet was not observed as it should have been; the ayah sets a boundary showing that a claimed Godward aim does not excuse a form of labor not faithfully kept.
The one who withholds and regards himself self-sufficient begins the opposite course of striving, reversing both giving and dependence upon the Lord.
Denying the best promise supplies the wrong destination behind the withholding and self-sufficiency of 92:8.
God will ease that person toward hardship, making the trajectory of misdirected effort the inverse of the ease promised in 92:7.
Those who make the balanced request of 2:201 have a share of what they earned, joining Godward asking to accountable human acquisition; its force depends on the preceding prayer.
The Prophet is to glorify God during the night and as the stars retreat, continuing 52:48's command to praise when rising into a repeated daily rhythm.
The Prophet must remember his Lord's name morning and evening, establishing the daily recurrence within which 76:26 places prolonged night worship.
Night prostration and long glorification continue the morning-evening remembrance of 76:25, giving sustained duration to the command to labor toward the Lord.
The Prophet is told to persevere because God's promise is true, seek forgiveness, and glorify his Lord evening and morning; endurance opens into a recurring cycle of Lordward acts.
